TECHNICAL GUIDE / SENSING

Camera vs sonar for underwater inspection

The right comparison starts with the inspection question, not the sensor name.

Prepare these inputs

  • Visibility and suspended material
  • Target size and inspection distance
  • Required detection and measurement
  • Position and reporting references
Industrial inspection guide

The short answer

Use a camera when water clarity and lighting let the operator see surface detail at the working distance. Add imaging sonar when visibility is poor, to navigate and recognise structures acoustically. Many inspections combine both: sonar to find the target, the camera for close visual evidence.

What a camera contributes

Optical video can show recognizable surface detail, markings and material appearance when light and water clarity allow. Lighting position, suspended particles, standoff distance and camera control affect what the operator can interpret.

A sharp image does not automatically provide scaled dimensions. Measurement needs an appropriate reference or calibrated method.

What imaging sonar contributes

Sonar uses acoustic information and can be useful for navigation and feature recognition where optical visibility is poor. Interpretation depends on the sonar type, frequency, geometry and target.

Imaging, profiling and bathymetric sonar serve different purposes. An optional sonar interface is not proof that a particular sensor or reporting workflow has been integrated.

Why a combined package may be appropriate

Sonar may help the operator approach or find a target; the camera may then provide local visual detail. Confirm that both data streams can be recorded, referenced and interpreted for the actual defect or condition.

Ask for task-relevant samples

Request footage and acoustic data from comparable visibility, geometry and target conditions. Agree what must be detected, how it will be located and what counts as acceptable evidence.

Questions for the sensing review
RequirementOptical reviewAcoustic review
Surface appearanceVisibility, lighting and usable standoffWhether the target has a relevant acoustic signature
NavigationAvailable scene detailField of view, range and feature recognition
MeasurementScale reference or calibrated methodSensor type, geometry and expected uncertainty
ReportingVideo, stills and annotationsRecorded formats and location reference
